## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — Starting Fresh? Run This First
If you're jumping into this module on a new day, or `raw_data` and
`raw_metadata` aren't in your environment, run this once before continuing:

```r
#| eval: false
metadata_url  <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv"
rawcounts_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv"

download.file(metadata_url,  destfile = "raw_data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
download.file(rawcounts_url, destfile = "raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")

raw_metadata <- read.csv("raw_data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
raw_data     <- read.csv("raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-live"></span> Browser Only Version — Load Straight From the URL
No persistent filesystem here, so skip the download step and read
directly from the source instead:

```{webr-r}
raw_metadata <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
raw_data     <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")
```
:::

You will almost certainly write code with an AI's help, starting the
moment you leave this course — maybe you already do. That's not a
problem this course is trying to talk you out of. The problem is
narrower, and it's the same problem every other arc has been circling:
**code that runs is not the same thing as code you understand, can
verify, and can hand to someone else.** An AI makes it easier than ever
to produce code that runs. It does nothing, on its own, to make that
code reproducible — that part is still entirely on you.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — Runs ≠ Correct
An AI assistant will confidently hand you a function that executes
without error and returns the wrong answer. It can invent a function
that doesn't exist, use a real function's arguments in the wrong order,
or quietly reach for an outdated package instead of its modern
replacement. None of these mistakes announce themselves — they look
exactly as confident as a correct answer.
:::

## Evaluating AI-Generated Code: A Worked Example

Before you try this yourself, here's what evaluating AI output actually
looks like, step by step. Suppose you'd asked an AI assistant:

> "Write an R function that takes a data frame and a column name, and
> returns the number of values in that column below 10."

And it handed back this:

```{webr-r}
count_low_values <- function(df, col_name) {
  sum(df[[col_name]] < 10)
}

count_low_values(raw_data, "GSM3119015")
```

It runs. It returns a number. Is that enough?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — The AI Code Checklist
Run this same checklist on every piece of AI-generated code before it
goes anywhere near a real analysis — all five items are habits this
course has already built, just aimed at a new source of code:

1. **Does it run?** — the lowest bar, and the only one an AI's confidence
   guarantees.
2. **Do you understand every line?** — if not, that's the signal to ask
   the AI to explain it, not to accept it on faith (Arc 3: reading error
   messages applies here too, since you can't debug what you don't
   understand).
3. **Is it documented in *your* words** — your Quarto doc explaining what
   it does and why, independent of whatever comments the AI added
   itself? (Arc 2)
4. **Is it committed**, with a message describing what changed and why?
   (Arc 6)
5. **Does `renv::snapshot()` capture every package it pulled in** — not
   just the ones you already had? (Arc 1)

Running the example above through this list: it executes (1), it's
simple enough to understand fully (2) — but it silently drops every `NA`
without flagging that it did, which is exactly the Arc 3 lesson about
`na.rm` and missing values resurfacing in new clothes. An AI didn't know
to ask whether that silence was intentional. You have to.
:::

```{webr-r}
# The same function, checked against what we already know about this column
anyNA(raw_data$GSM3119015)
count_low_values(raw_data, "GSM3119015")
```

## Your Turn: Get Code From an AI, Then Audit It

Open Claude, ChatGPT, or whichever assistant you use, and ask it this:

> "Write an R function called `flag_mid_expression` that takes a data
> frame, a column name, a low threshold, and a high threshold, and
> returns `TRUE` for every value strictly between the two thresholds —
> and `FALSE` for everything else, including missing values."

Paste whatever it gives you into the cell below, in place of the
placeholder, and run it.

```{webr-r}
# TODO: replace this placeholder with whatever your AI assistant gave you
flag_mid_expression <- function(df, col_name, low, high) {
  df[[col_name]] > low & df[[col_name]] < high
}

flag_mid_expression(raw_data, "GSM3119015", low = 10, high = 1000)
```

Now run it through the checklist above. Specifically:

- Does it correctly return `FALSE` — not `NA` — for missing values?
  (`anyNA(raw_data$GSM3119015)` told you there's at least one to test
  this against.)
- Do you understand every operator it used?
- Could you explain, out loud, what this function does to someone who's
  never seen it?

<details>
<summary>One possible correct version</summary>

```r
flag_mid_expression <- function(df, col_name, low, high) {
  values <- df[[col_name]]
  result <- values > low & values < high
  result[is.na(values)] <- FALSE
  result
}
```

Many AI assistants will skip the `NA` handling entirely — `>` and `<`
against `NA` silently return `NA`, not `FALSE`. If what you pasted did
that, you've just caught exactly the kind of error this checklist exists
to catch.
</details>

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tour"></span> Code Tour — Three Ways AI-Generated R Code Fails Quietly
Three real patterns worth recognizing on sight. Each runs if you run it
in your own browser cell — try each one before reading what's wrong.

**1. The invented function.** AI assistants sometimes blend real function
names with plausible-sounding ones that don't exist:

```{webr-r}
mean_no_na(raw_data$GSM3119015)
```

This fails loudly — `could not find function` — which is actually the
easy case. The real function is `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`; `mean_no_na()`
was never real.

**2. The misordered argument.** Unlike many functions, `grepl()` expects
*pattern* first, *text to search* second — reverse them and the function
still runs, it just silently matches nothing:

```{webr-r}
grepl(raw_metadata$characteristics, "homecage")  # wrong order — runs, finds nothing
grepl("homecage", raw_metadata$characteristics)  # correct order
```

Compare the two outputs. The first returns all `FALSE`. Nothing about
that result looks like an error.

**3. The outdated package.** Ask an AI for a "group and summarize"
operation in R and it may reach for the `plyr` package — a real
tool, but one `dplyr` (which this course has used throughout Arc 5)
has almost entirely replaced:

```r
#| eval: false
library(plyr)
ddply(raw_metadata, "genotype", summarise, n = length(genotype))
```

This isn't wrong, exactly — it's dated. `plyr` is no longer actively
maintained, and its functions can conflict with `dplyr` if both are
loaded. The equivalent you already know:

```{webr-r}
raw_metadata %>%
  count(genotype)
```

An AI trained on years of public code will sometimes hand you the
2014 answer to a question that has a better 2024 answer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — Getting Better Code Out of an AI
A vague prompt gets a vague — or wrong — answer. A few habits that
consistently produce better code:

- **Be specific about shape and edge cases** — "returns `FALSE` for
  missing values" is something you have to ask for; it's rarely assumed.
- **Give it real context** — paste the actual column names or a few
  real rows, instead of describing your data in the abstract.
- **Ask it to explain its own code back to you** — if the explanation
  doesn't match what the code actually does, that mismatch is worth
  investigating before you trust either one.
- **Treat the first answer as a draft** — asking a follow-up ("what
  happens here if the column has an `NA`?") often surfaces exactly the
  kind of gap this arc has been pointing at.

For more on getting useful results from Claude specifically, Anthropic's
prompting documentation is at
[docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — Going Further: Claude Code
Everything in this arc used chat-based AI — you asked a question, got code
back, and pasted it in yourself. A coding agent like Claude Code goes a
step further: it reads your project's files directly, writes code into
them, runs it, and fixes its own errors. The checklist from this arc
doesn't change — it's the same "Claude does, you decide" split — it just
needs sharper tools, since an agent can do far more per turn than a chat
window ever could. ARCS's companion class, *Analyzing Research Data with
Claude Code*, walks through exactly that: permission rules that enforce
what advice alone can't, a plan-before-you-code workflow, and a required
human review step before anything is trusted. If this arc made you want
to go further, that's the natural next stop.
:::

## What We Did, and Why

**What we built:** evaluated a worked AI-generated function against the
five-point checklist, requested a function of your own from an AI tool
and audited it the same way, and diagnosed three common, quiet failure
patterns in AI-generated R code.

**Why it matters:** nothing in this arc was a new R skill — every piece
of the checklist was something Arcs 1, 2, 3, and 6 already built. What's
new is the source of the code. The repo is the reproducible artifact —
whether you wrote every line of it yourself, or an AI handed you the
first draft. The habits from this entire course are what make that true
either way.
